website = | footnotes = }} '''Exchange Place''' is a district of [[Downtown Jersey City]], [[New Jersey]] that is sometimes referred to as [[Wall Street West]] due to the concentration of financial companies that have offices there. The namesake is a square, about 200 feet long, at the foot of Montgomery Street at the [[Hudson Waterfront|waterfront]] of the [[Hudson River]]. This square was created by landfilling the shore at [[Paulus Hook]], and has been a major transportation hub since the colonial era.{{cite web |url=http://www.njcu.edu/programs/jchistory/Pages/E_Pages/Exchange_Place.htm |title=Exchange Place |work=Jersey City Past and Present |publisher=New Jersey City University |first1=Carmela |last1=Karnoutsos |first2=Patrick |last2=Shalhoub |year=2007 |access-date=February 16, 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20040814221758/http://www.njcu.edu/programs/jchistory/Pages/E_Pages/Exchange_Place.htm |archive-date=August 14, 2004 |url-status=dead }} == Vicinity == [[File:Jersey City.JPG|thumb|upright=1.1|Aerial view of Exchange Place in 2010]] [[File:911 from the Jersey City the place where the twin towers were.jpg|thumb|upright=1.1|[[Jersey City 9/11 Memorial]]]] [[File:NYC Downtown Manhattan Skyline seen from Paulus Hook 2020-02-03 IMG 7973 FRD.jpg|thumb|upright=1.1|[[Lower Manhattan]] skyline as seen from Exchange Place]] A high concentration of [[List of tallest buildings in Jersey City|highrise office and residential buildings in the city]] are located in the district radiating from Exchange Place, which since the 1990s has overtaken [[Journal Square]] as [[Hudson County]]'s major business district and become a major business center along the redeveloped waterfronts in the [[Port of New York and New Jersey]]. The Mack-Cali building is host to several nesting sites for [[peregrine falcon]]s. The [[Hudson River Waterfront Walkway]] crosses Exchange, the other side of which is [[J. Owen Grundy|J. Owen Grundy Park]], extending into the [[North River (Hudson River)|Hudson River]]. The [[Katyń Memorial (Jersey City)|Katyń Memorial]] by [[Polish American|Polish-American]] artist [[Andrzej Pitynski]] is the first memorial of its kind to be raised on American soil to honor the dead of the [[Katyn massacre|Katyń Forest massacre]].{{cite news | work=[[The Record (North Jersey)|The Record]] | date=June 6, 1991 | last=Stoltzfus | first=Duane | title=Statue Erected as Memorial to Victims of Katyn Massacre}} In early May 2018, Holocaust survivor [[Edward Mosberg]] co-signed a letter asking Jersey City Mayor [[Steven Fulop]] not to remove the Katyń Memorial from Exchange Place in the city, writing: "The memory of the Katyn massacre is an important part of the memory and memories of the Holocaust and we encourage you to reconsider your decision to remove this monument."{{Cite web|url=https://dzieje.pl/aktualnosci/polonia-zbulwersowana-planami-usuniecia-pomnika-katynskiego-z-placu-w-jersey-city|title=Polonia zbulwersowana planami usunięcia pomnika katyńskiego z placu w Jersey City|date=May 5, 2018|website=dzieje.pl}} To the south are [[New York Waterway]]'s Paulus Hook Ferry Terminal, and the two tallest buildings in New Jersey; the [[30 Hudson Street|Goldman Sachs Tower]] and [[99 Hudson Street|99 Hudson]]. The [[Colgate Clock (New Jersey)|Colgate Clock]], promoted by [[Colgate-Palmolive]] as the largest in the world, faces [[Battery Park (New York)|Battery Park]] in lower Manhattan. The clock, which is {{convert|50|ft|m}} in diameter with a minute hand weighing 2,200 pounds, was erected in 1924 to replace a [[Colgate Clock (Indiana)|smaller one]] that was relocated to a plant in [[Jeffersonville, Indiana]].{{cite news | work=The New York Times | date=July 9, 1989 | last=Lyons | first=Richard | title=Jersey City Landmark; Now It's Time to Move the Colgate Clock | url=https://www.nytimes.com/1989/07/09/realestate/postings-jersey-city-landmark-now-it-s-time-to-move-the-colgate-clock.html?pagewanted=1 | access-date=January 30, 2010}} The riverfront promenade, which provides vistas of [[Lower Manhattan]], continues along the [[Morris Canal|Morris Canal Little Basin]], part of [[Liberty State Park]]. To the north is the former warehouse now housing [[Harborside Financial Center]]. == History == As early as July 1764History of the County of Hudson, New Jersey: From Its Earliest Settlement to the Present Time, Charles Hardenburg Winfield, pg. 243-246, Kennard & Hay Stationery M'fg and Print. Company, 1874 a ferry began operating from [[Paulus Hook, Jersey City|Paulus Hook]] to Mesier's dock which was located at the foot of Courtland Street (where [[Cortland Street Ferry Depot]] would be built)''Railroad Ferries of the Hudson: And Stories of a Deckhand'', by, Raymond J. Baxter, Arthur G. Adams, pg. 64, 1999, Fordham University Press, 978-0823219544 and where [[Battery Park City Ferry Terminal]] is located today. The first steam ferry service in [[Port of New York and New Jersey|New York Harbor]] and the world was established in 1812 by [[Robert Livingston (1746-1813)]] and [[Robert Fulton]] and traveled between [[Paulus Hook]] and Cortlandt Street in [[Manhattan]].Cudahy, Brian J. [https://books.google.com/books?id=cFR56pF1JaUC&pg=PA466 ''Over and Back''] New York: Fordham University Press, 1990. pp.20-24,360,362 The ferry dock stood at the head of the important highway to [[Newark, New Jersey|Newark]] (and points west and south) established in 1795.John T. Cunningham, ''Newark''. Newark: New Jersey Historical Society, 1966. p84-85. The ferry in turn influenced the location of the terminal of the [[New Jersey Railroad]], which opened in 1838 running from the ferry dock via Newark to [[New Brunswick, New Jersey|New Brunswick]]. The railroad purchased the ferry operation in 1853Brian J. Cudahy, ''Over and Back''. New York: Fordham University Press, 1990. p59. and in 1858 built a much-needed larger [[Intermodal passenger transport|intermodal terminal]]. After acquiring the railroad in 1871, the [[Pennsylvania Railroad]] replaced the [[Exchange Place (PRR station)|terminal]] in 1876 and yet again in 1888–1892.Carl Condit, ''The Port of New York''. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1980. v1 p46-52,152-168. Passengers could move directly between the trains and ferries without going outside (a similar plan can still be seen today at [[Hoboken Terminal]]). The railroad referred to the location simply as Jersey City, and if necessary to distinguish it from other railroads' terminals, as the [[Exchange Place (PRR station)|Pennsylvania station]]. It was probably the [[Tram|street railways]], the local transportation in Jersey City, that first needed to identify the location more precisely as Exchange Place.American railroad Journal Vol 32, June 18, 1859 Beginning with [[horsecar]]s in 1860, the local network connected the ferry with neighborhoods in the city and nearby towns. An off-street terminal called "Exchange Place" was established in 1891. It was almost at the water's edge, across the street from the [[Exchange Place (PRR station)|Pennsylvania Railroad terminal]] and with easy access to the ferries.John Harrington Riley, ''The Newark City Subway Lines''. 1987. p194. Cars with signs reading EXCHANGE PLACE could be seen all over town. In 1901, the privately held land was given to the city by the PRR.{{cite news |title=Settlement in the Seaboard Litigation; Decision of Daniel S. Lamont as the Arbitrator |url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/abstract.html?res=9E0DE2DE103DEE32A25753C2A9649C946097D6CF |newspaper=The New York Times |date=February 20, 1901 |access-date=February 25, 2011}} The [[Hudson and Manhattan Railroad Company|Hudson and Manhattan Railroad]] opened its tunnels from Exchange Place to New York in 1910.Carl Condit, ''The Port of New York''. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1980. v1 p247-254.{{Cite news | title = 40,000 celebrate new tubes opening | newspaper = New York Times | date = July 20, 1909 | url = https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1909/07/20/101891053.pdf | access-date = December 31, 2010}} Significantly, the station was at first called "Pennsylvania Railroad Station", not Exchange Place,''Official Guide of the Railways''. January 1910, p.68. but by 1916 the name was expanded to include "Exchange Place".''Official Guide of the Railways''. June 1916, p.397. By 1926 the H & M station was simply "Exchange Place".''Official Guide of the Railways''. February 1926, p.308. The Pennsylvania Railroad did not officially give in until some years later, but all the stations, and the neighborhood, were firmly known as Exchange Place by the 1920s. For many years the location functioned similarly to [[Hudson Place (Hoboken)|Hudson Place]], farther up the Hudson waterfront, as a terminus for the many [[tram|trolley]] lines which crisscrossed [[Hudson County]], as well as for those which traveled farther, from destinations such as the [[Newark Public Service Terminal]], or the [[Paterson Broadway Bus Terminal|Broadway Terminal]] in Paterson. At one time more than ten lines operated by the [[Public Service Railway]] originated/terminated here. The substitution of rail lines with busses, colloquially known as [[bustitution]], was completed in 1949.French, Kenneth, ''Images of Rail:'' Railroads of Hoboken and Jersey City, Arcadia Publishing, 2002, p125, {{ISBN|978-0-7385-0966-2}} Ferry services were also discontinued in 1949,Brian J. Cudahy, ''Over and Back''. New York: Fordham University Press, 1990. p362. and while the Pennsylvania Railroad service dwindled after the opening of [[Pennsylvania Station (New York City)|Penn Station]] in New York in 1910, it did not end until 1962.Carl Condit, ''The Port of New York''. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1981. v2 p228. Following the end of service on the [[Jersey City Branch]], the remains of the large terminal were demolished, leaving a large open space on the waterfront. This and the elimination of other railroad passenger and freight yards along the river during the 1960s and 1970s opened up the land that would be used for redevelopment. The continued use of the name "Exchange Place" was based on the Hudson and Manhattan station ([[Port Authority Trans-Hudson|PATH]] since 1962) and signs on the bus routes that had replaced the trolleys. Since 2000, both a trolley service, in the form of the [[Hudson–Bergen Light Rail]], and a ferry service, provided by [[NY Waterway]] at the Paulus Hook Hook Ferry Terminal, have been restored. It is also the terminus for several New Jersey Transit and privately operated bus routes. == Transportation == [[File:Hudson bergen exchange place.jpg|thumb|upright=1.1|Hudson–Bergen Light Rail trains traveling between stations]] ===Pennsylvania Railroad Station=== {{For|the former [[Pennsylvania Railroad]] terminal |Exchange Place (PRR station)}} ===PATH=== [[Port Authority Trans Hudson|PATH]] service from [[Exchange Place (PATH station)|Exchange Place]] runs east to the [[World Trade Center (PATH station)|World Trade Center]], north to [[Hoboken Terminal]], and west to [[Journal Square Transportation Center|Journal Square]] and [[Newark Penn Station]]. ===HBLR=== Three stations of the [[Hudson–Bergen Light Rail]] in the district are [[Harborside Financial Center (HBLR station)|Harborside Financial Center]], [[Essex Street (HBLR station)|Essex Street]] and [[Exchange Place (HBLR station)|Exchange Place]], where transfer to [[Port Authority Trans Hudson|PATH]] and ferry are possible. ===Paulus Hook Ferry Terminal=== [[File:Colgate-clock.jpg|250px|thumb|upright=1.1|[[Colgate Clock (New Jersey)|Colgate Clock]] and [[New York Waterway|Paulus Hook Ferry Terminal]]]] [[File:NYC Downtown Manhattan Skyline seen from Paulus Hook 2020-02-06 IMG 8003 FRD.jpg|thumb|upright=1.1|Ferry service departing Battery Park City (background) towards Paulus Hook (foreground)]] The ferry that started in 1764 became known as the [[Jersey City Ferry]], but after nearly 200 years of service, the last regular ferry service across the Hudson ended in the 1960s. [[Academy Bus]]{{Cite web |url=http://www.academybus.com/LinkClick.aspx?fileticket=Fk4oAzYzmHk%3d&tabid=71&mid=475 |title=Archived copy |access-date=April 20, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100413184920/http://www.academybus.com/LinkClick.aspx?fileticket=Fk4oAzYzmHk%3D&tabid=71&mid=475 |archive-date=April 13, 2010 |url-status=dead }} |'''[[Garden State Arts Center]]''' |limited peak service |} == In popular culture == The views provided along the waterfront are often featured as background images of [[New York City]] and [[One World Trade Center]] that have been used for [[Gmail]], [[WordPress.com|WordPress]], and [[Emporis]]. The [[EarthCam]] webcam for One World Trade Center, which is placed on top of the Hyatt Regency Hotel, is viewed by millions every week and is occasionally used by local TV news stations. The 1998 film [[Godzilla (1998 film)|Godzilla]] used the area that the [[30 Hudson Street|Goldman Sachs Tower]] currently occupies as the location for a military base. The Exchange Place PATH station was used to film an episode of [[Law & Order: Special Victims Unit]], and the ending of the film [[Sid and Nancy]] was shot in the vicinity of Exchange Place near [[Harborside (Jersey City)|Harborside]]. A segment of [[MTV]]'s "The Week in Rock" was filmed along the Exchange Place waterfront during an interview with [[Queen Latifah]]. The pier and its New York backdrop is commonly used in the 2021 series [[The Equalizer (2021 TV series)|''The Equalizer'']] as the location where Robyn and William privately meet. The view of [[Lower Manhattan]] from Exchange Place has been used for shots in the music video for [[Demi Lovato]]'s [[I Love Me (song)|I Love Me]] and in the lyric video for Afrojack and David Guetta's song [[Hero (Afrojack and David Guetta song)|Hero]]. ==See also== *[[List of Public Service Railway lines]] *[[List of ferries across the Hudson River to New York City]] == References == {{Reflist|2}} {{Jersey City, New Jersey}} {{New Jersey Transit Bus Operations}} {{Hudson County Transportation Network}} {{NYC surface transit}} [[Category:Neighborhoods in Jersey City, New Jersey]] [[Category:Financial districts in the United States|United States]] [[Category:Streets in Hudson County, New Jersey]] [[Category:Transportation in Hudson County, New Jersey]] [[Category:New Jersey streetcar lines]] [[Category:Bus transportation in New Jersey]] [[Category:NJ Transit Bus Operations]] [[Category:Transit hubs serving New Jersey]] [[Category:Redeveloped ports and waterfronts in the United States]] [[Category:Tourist attractions in Jersey City, New Jersey]]
